title: Basat and the One-Eyed Giant
author: Anonymous (Book of Dede Korkut), adapted by Lantern

source.name: Dede Korkut Kitabı, Dresden manuscript, 8th boy ("Basat depe gözi öldürdiği toyı beyân eder") — adapted into English by Lantern; plot taken from the Latin-letter transcription of the anonymous Dresden manuscript text on Turkish Wikisource, retold entirely in our own words (no modern edition or translation was copied)
source.license: Public domain (anonymous medieval source text); this English adaptation is by Lantern

summaryTr: Bir aslanın büyüttüğü Basat, Oğuzları korku içinde yaşatan, okun ve kılıcın işlemediği tek gözlü dev Tepegöz'ün karşısına çıkmaya karar verir. Dede Korkut Kitabı'nın sekizinci boyunun, kolay İngilizceyle yeniden anlatımı.
paragraphs: ## The Boy and the Lion

Long ago the Oghuz people lived on the wide grasslands. They moved from place to place with their horses, sheep and tents. Their great ruler was Bayındır Khan, and among his lords was an old, respected man called Aruz Koca. (In the old language, Koca means "elder".)

One night enemy riders came out of the dark. The camp woke up in terror, and there was no time to fight. The people took what they could carry and rode away across the plain. In the noise and the confusion, a small boy fell from a horse, and nobody saw it. He was Aruz Koca's younger son.
The child lay alone in the grass, crying. At dawn a lion found him. Strangely, the lion did not eat him. It carried him gently to its den and took care of him as if he were one of its own cubs.

Years passed. The enemy went away, and the Oghuz came back to their old land and put up their tents again. One morning the khan's horse-keeper came running with strange news. "My khan," he said, "a lion has come out of the reeds. It kills our horses. And it walks step by step, like a man!"
Aruz Koca listened carefully, and his face changed. "Wait," he said. "On the night we ran away, I lost a little boy. Perhaps this is my son."
The lords took their horses and rode to the lion's den. They drove the lion away and found a strong, dirty, wild-looking boy. They brought him to Aruz Koca's tent, and there was a great feast.
But the boy did not want to stay with them. Again and again he escaped and went back to the lion's bed, and again and again the men had to fetch him.

At last the old storyteller Dede Korkut came. He was the wisest man of the Oghuz. He gave names to children, he gave advice to lords, and everybody listened when he spoke. He sat down beside the boy and spoke kindly.

"My son, you are a human being, not an animal," he said. "Do not spend your life with beasts. Come and ride a good horse. Ride and hunt with brave young men. Your big brother is Kıyan Selçuk. Your name is Basat from now on. I give you this name, and may God give you a long life."

The boy looked at the old man for a long time. Then he stayed. He learned to ride, to shoot a bow and to use a sword, and the boy who had been raised by a lion became one of the strongest young warriors of the Oghuz.
## The Shepherd and the Spring
Every summer the Oghuz drove their flocks up to the cool pastures in the mountains. Aruz Koca had a shepherd called Sarı, a strong, rough man who always led his sheep a little ahead of the tribe.

On the road there was a spring called Uzun Bınar, the Long Spring. Its water was cold and clear, and everybody knew it. That year, peris had made camp beside it. Peris are beautiful spirits from the old stories of the East. They have wings, and they can fly like birds.

The shepherd was walking quietly when all of a sudden the sheep became afraid and began to run in every direction. He hurried ahead to see what was wrong. By the water he saw a group of peri girls with their wings joined together, ready to fly up. He threw his heavy cloak over them and caught one of the girls. It was a cruel and foolish thing to do. The girl cried out and struggled, but the frightened sheep were running off toward the hills, and the shepherd had to let her go and run after them.

The peri girl beat her wings and rose into the air. "Shepherd!" she called down. "One year from today I will have something that belongs to you. Come back to this place and take it. But remember this: you have brought trouble to the Oghuz."
The shepherd's face turned pale. He did not understand everything she said, but he understood that he had done wrong.

A year went by. Again the Oghuz moved to the summer pastures, and again the sheep took fright near the Long Spring. The shepherd ran ahead and saw something lying next to the water. It was not an animal, and it was not a person. It was a big, round lump, and it shone and trembled in the sun. The peri girl was standing beside it.
"Shepherd, here is what is yours," she said. "Take it. But you have brought trouble to the Oghuz."

The shepherd was much too frightened to touch it. He stepped back. Then he put a stone into his sling and threw it at the lump. It grew a little bigger. He threw another stone, and it grew bigger again. The shepherd dropped his sling and ran after his sheep as fast as he could.

Not long after that, Bayındır Khan came to the same spring with his lords. They were out hunting. When they saw the strange thing by the water, they stopped their horses and stared. Nobody could tell which end was the head and which was the tail. A young man kicked it, and the more he kicked, the bigger it grew. Other young men kicked it too, and it only went on growing.

At last old Aruz Koca got down from his horse. He pushed his spur into the lump, and it split open. A boy came out of it. He looked like any other child, except for one thing: on the top of his head, in the middle, there was a single large eye.
Aruz Koca picked up the child and wrapped him in the skirt of his coat. "My khan," he said, "please give this boy to me. I will bring him up as my own son."
"He is yours," said Bayındır Khan.
So the one-eyed boy went home with Aruz Koca. The people called him Tepegöz, which means "Top-Eye", because his eye was on the top of his head.
## The Giant of the Mountain

Aruz Koca found a nurse for the baby, a woman who could feed him with her milk. The first time Tepegöz drank, he took her milk. The second time he took her blood. The third time he took her life. Other women came, one after another, and the same thing happened to each of them. At last the people understood that no woman could be his nurse. They fed him with animal milk, but a whole big pot a day was not enough for him.

He grew very fast. Soon he could walk, and then he began to play with the other children of the camp. But he did not play gently. He bit their ears and their noses, and the children ran home crying. The angry, frightened parents went to Aruz Koca and complained, and some of them wept in front of him.

Aruz Koca shouted at the boy, punished him and told him never to hurt anyone again. It did no good. Tepegöz paid no attention to anybody. In the end Aruz Koca, with a heavy heart, drove him out of the house.
The boy walked away alone. That same day his mother, the peri, came to him. She put a ring on his finger and said, "My son, let no arrow go into your body, and let no sword cut your skin."

With that ring Tepegöz was stronger than any man. He went up a high mountain and made it his home. He stopped travellers on the road and carried them off, and soon he was the worst robber the Oghuz had ever known. The Oghuz sent men against him, but arrows broke on his body, swords could not cut him and spears would not go in. Shepherds and whole families disappeared. Before long he began to eat the people he caught.

At last the Oghuz gathered all their warriors and rode against him together. Tepegöz saw them coming. He roared, tore a tree out of the ground and swung it, and fifty or sixty men fell. Great heroes were lost in that fight. Kara Göne, the brother of the famous Kazan Beg, was beaten. (Beg means "lord".) Old Aruz Koca was hurt so badly that he coughed up blood. And his elder son, Kıyan Selçuk, never came home.
The Oghuz tried to run away from the giant. Seven times they packed their tents and fled, and seven times Tepegöz ran ahead, cut off the road and drove them back to the place they had left.
In their trouble they sent for Dede Korkut. "Go to him," they said. "We cannot fight him any more. Ask him what he wants."
Dede Korkut climbed the mountain alone and greeted the giant politely. "Tepegöz," he said, "the Oghuz are beaten. Let them pay you a price every day, and leave them in peace."
"Give me sixty men a day to eat," said Tepegöz.
"At that rate," said Dede Korkut, "you will soon have no men left to eat. Let them give you two men and five hundred sheep every day."
Tepegöz thought about it. "Good," he said. "Two men a day. But I want a cook. Let him cook for me, and I will eat."
Dede Korkut went back down and told the Oghuz. They chose two old men, Yünlü Koca and Yapagulu Koca, to be the giant's cooks. They had no other choice.

From that day on, two men and five hundred sheep went up the mountain every morning. Each family had to give a son in turn. A man with four sons gave one and had three left. A man with three gave one and had two left. A man with two gave one and had one left. And then the turn came round again.
## Basat Comes Home

There was a man named Kapak Han who had two sons. He had already given one to the giant, and now the turn had come for the other. The boy's mother wept and asked everyone for help, but nobody could do anything. Then she remembered something. "Aruz Koca's son Basat has been away on a raid," she said. "Perhaps he has come back. If he gives me a prisoner, I can send the prisoner instead of my boy."
Basat had just returned from a long raid, and he was sitting in front of his tent when he saw a woman coming across the grass. She came in, greeted him and burst into tears.
"Basat, son of Aruz," she said, "your name is known in the inner Oghuz and in the outer Oghuz. Help me!"
"What do you want, mother?" he asked kindly.

"A terrible creature has risen among us," she said. "Swords cannot cut him, and arrows cannot go into him. Seven times he drove the Oghuz from their camp. He hurt your white-bearded father so badly that he coughed up blood. He killed your brother Kıyan Selçuk. Now he takes two men and five hundred sheep every day. I had two sons, and I gave one, and now the turn has come back to me. Help me, Basat!"

Basat's dark eyes filled with tears. He thought of his brother, and he spoke in a low voice. "My brother, that cruel creature took you away from us. He made our father cry, and he made our mother's heart break." Then he gave the woman a prisoner from his raid. "Go," he said. "Save your son."

The woman took the prisoner and gave him up in place of her son. Then, full of joy, she ran to Aruz Koca's tent. "Your son has come home!" she cried. Aruz Koca was overjoyed. He rode out to meet Basat with all the lords of the Oghuz. Basat kissed his father's hand, and the two of them wept together. Then he went to his mother's house, and she held him tight. That night there was a feast with plenty to eat and drink.
In the middle of the feast Basat stood up. "My lords," he said, "for my brother's sake I will fight Tepegöz. What do you say?"

For a moment nobody spoke. Then Kazan Beg, the greatest warrior of the Oghuz, shook his head. "I chased him over the black mountains and through the thick reeds," he said, "and I could not catch him. Be a better man than I was, Basat, and do not make your white-bearded father cry again."
Aruz Koca took his son's hand. "My son," he said, "do not leave my house empty. Do me this kindness: do not go."
"No, my dear white-bearded father," said Basat. "I must go."

He had made up his mind, and nothing could change it. He put a handful of arrows in his belt and hung his sword at his side. He hung a small charm with a prayer inside it around his neck, and he carried his bow across his shoulder. He tucked his coat into his belt, kissed the hands of his father and his mother and asked for their blessing. "Stay well," he said, and he set off.
## The Red-Hot Spit

Tepegöz lived in a cave at the foot of a great rock, which the Oghuz called the Slaughter Rock. When Basat arrived, he found the giant sitting alone with his back to the sun. The two old cooks were working near the fire.

Basat took an arrow, pulled his bow and shot the giant in the side. The arrow broke into pieces. He shot a second arrow, and it broke too. Tepegöz did not even turn his head. "The flies of this place are tiring me," he said to the old men.

Basat shot once more. This time a small piece of the arrow landed in front of the giant. Tepegöz jumped up and looked around. When he saw Basat, he clapped his hands and laughed. "Look at this!" he said to the cooks. "The Oghuz have sent me a little something before dinner!"

He took Basat by the throat, carried him to his bed and pushed him into the top of his boot like a pocket. "Old men," he said, "wake me at dinner time. I will eat this one raw." And he went back to sleep.
Basat lay in the dark leather and did not move. He had a dagger at his belt. Very carefully, he cut the leather and climbed out. The giant went on snoring.
"Old men," Basat whispered, "tell me. How can this creature die?" "We do not know," they whispered back. "His body is like stone. But he has no soft flesh anywhere except in his eye."

Basat went to the giant's face and gently lifted the eyelid with his finger. They were right. The eye was soft and wet. "Old men," he said, "put the iron spits in the fire and let them get hot." The cooks pushed the long spits into the fire and blew on the flames. Soon the iron glowed red.
Basat took the hottest spit in both hands. He whispered a short prayer, calling on God and on the Prophet Muhammad. Then, with all his strength, he pushed the glowing spit into the giant's eye.

Tepegöz screamed. The sound was so loud that the mountains and the rocks shook. Basat jumped away and ran into the back of the cave, where hundreds of sheep were waiting in the dark. He pushed in among them and lay still.

Blind and mad with pain, the giant knew where Basat had gone. He went to the cave mouth and stood with one foot on each side of the entrance. "Sheep!" he roared. "Come out one by one!" One by one they came out, and he felt every head with his hands. "Come out, my old ram," he called.

Basat saw that he could not get past those hands, so he did something clever. He caught the biggest ram, killed it quickly and took off its skin with great care, leaving the head and the tail on it. Then he put the skin around himself like a coat and crept to the cave mouth on his hands and knees.

The giant's hands felt the head, the horns and the thick wool. "Ah, my old ram," he said, "you know where my death comes from. I will throw you against the wall so hard that your tail will make it greasy!" Basat pushed the ram's head into the giant's hands. Tepegöz took hold of the horns and lifted them high. But the horns and the skin stayed in his hands, and Basat slipped out between his legs and ran into the sunlight.
## The Last Sword
The giant threw the horns on the ground. "Boy, are you free?" he cried. "God has saved me," Basat answered.

Tepegöz was silent for a moment. Then he spoke in a friendly voice. "Do you see my ring lying there? Take it and put it on your finger," he said. "Then no arrow and no sword will ever hurt you." Basat took the ring and slipped it on. "Did you put it on?" asked the giant. "I did," said Basat.

At once Tepegöz drew his dagger and struck. The blade cut through Basat's coat, but Basat sprang away and stood in the open. He looked at his hand. The ring was not there. It was still lying under the giant's foot, and the giant had only played a trick on his eyes.
"Are you free now?" asked the giant. "God has saved me," said Basat again. "Do you see that building with the round roof?" said the giant. "That is my treasure house. Go in and look at my gold."
Basat went inside. Gold coins lay there in great piles, shining in the dim light. He stood and stared, and for a moment he forgot where he was. Behind him the giant pulled the heavy door shut.

"Are you inside?" cried Tepegöz. "I am," said Basat. "Then I will hit this building with my sword," said the giant, "and you will be crushed together with the dome." Basat spoke the words of his faith: "There is no god but God." At that moment the dome split open, and seven doors appeared in its walls. Basat ran out through one of them. Tepegöz pushed his arm into the building and kicked it so hard that the whole dome turned upside down.

"Are you free?" the giant shouted. "God has saved me," said Basat. "There is no death for you," said Tepegöz. "Look at that cave over there. Two swords hang in it. One is in a scabbard, and one has no scabbard. The one without a scabbard will cut off my head. Go and bring it, and kill me."

Basat walked to the mouth of the cave. A sword without a scabbard hung there from a chain, and it was never still. It swung down and up, down and up. "I will not just grab this," thought Basat. He drew his own sword and held it out. The hanging blade cut it in two. He fetched a thick branch and held that out. It was cut in two as well. "So that was the giant's plan," he said to himself.

He took his bow and aimed at the chain. His arrow struck it, the chain broke, and the sword fell into the mud and lay there. Basat pulled it out carefully, slid it into a scabbard and held it tightly by the handle. Then he walked back to the giant.

"How are you now, Tepegöz?" he asked. "Boy, have you not died yet?" said the giant. "God has saved me." Tepegöz said nothing for a long time. At last he spoke sadly. "It seems there is no death for you."

Then he began to sing, and his song was about his eye. "My eye, my eye, my only eye! With one eye I broke the Oghuz. Young man, you have taken me from my eye. May God take you from your sweet life! Now I know the pain of the eye. May God let no hero ever know it."

He lifted his blind face. "Who are you?" he asked. "Who is your lord, and what is your father's name? A brave man should not hide his name." "My lord is Bayındır Khan," said Basat. "My father is Aruz Koca, and my name is Basat."
"Brother, do not kill me!" said the giant.

"You made my white-bearded father cry," said Basat. "You broke my mother's heart. You killed my brother Kıyan, and you left his wife alone and his little children without a father. I will not leave this place until I have put my sword to your neck, once and for all."
Basat rose like a young bull. He pushed the giant down on his knees, and with the giant's own sword he struck the last blow. The terror of the Oghuz was over.

Basat called the two old cooks and sent them to the Oghuz with the good news. They rode away on grey horses, and the news ran through all the land. A rider galloped to Aruz Koca's house. "Good news!" he cried. "Your son has crushed Tepegöz!"
The lords of the Oghuz hurried to the Slaughter Rock. They carried the giant's head into the middle of the field, so that everyone could see he was really dead.

Then Dede Korkut came. He took up his kopuz, the old stringed instrument of the Oghuz, and played joyful music, and he sang of everything that had happened to the heroes. Then he blessed Basat. "You took your brother's revenge with courage, and you freed the Oghuz from this pain. When you come to a black mountain, may it let you pass. When you come to a river of blood, may it give you a way across."
That, my khan, is the story of Basat, the boy raised by a lion, and how he freed his people from the One-Eyed Giant.

glossary.koca: ihtiyar, yaşlı ve saygın kişi (Aruz Koca'daki gibi)
glossary.peri: peri (eski doğu masallarında kanatlı, güzel ruh)
glossary.spit: şiş (et kızartmak için uzun demir çubuk)

phrases.tr: kesin olarak, bir kez ve tamamen

quiz.q: Who found the little boy who fell from the horse in the night?
quiz.explainTr: Düşen küçük çocuğu bir aslan bulur; onu yemez, yuvasına götürüp kendi yavrusuymuş gibi bakar.

quiz.q: What did Tepegöz's peri mother give him?
options: A ring that kept arrows and swords away
quiz.explainTr: Peri anne oğlunun parmağına bir yüzük takar; bu yüzük sayesinde ok batmaz, kılıç kesmez.

quiz.q: Why did the old woman come to Basat's tent?
options: She wanted him to save her son from the giant
She wanted to sell him some sheep
She had a message from Dede Korkut
She wanted him to marry her daughter
quiz.explainTr: Kadının iki oğlundan biri devin yemeği olarak verilmişti; sıra ikincisine gelince yardım için Basat'a gider.

quiz.q: How did Basat get out of the cave after he had blinded the giant?
options: He ran out in the dark
He hid inside the skin of a ram
quiz.explainTr: Basat bir koçun derisini giyer; dev boynuzu tutup kaldırınca deri elinde kalır, Basat da bacaklarının arasından kaçar.

quiz.q: What did Basat use to give the giant the final blow?
quiz.explainTr: Ok ve kılıç devi kesmez; Basat sonunda devin kendi kılıcını alıp son darbeyi vurur.
